boar.e: From Middle English bor, boor, from Old English bār, from Proto-West Germanic *bair.
boar.g: A wild boar (Sus scrofa), the wild ancestor of the domesticated pig.

board.e: From Middle English boord, boorde, bord, bourd, burd, from Old English bord, from Proto-West Germanic *bord, from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board, plank; edge; table”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰers- (“tip, top”) + *-dʰeti or *bʰerH- (“to pierce; to strike”) + *-dʰeti. The senses "food" and "council" are by metonymy from the sense "table".
board.g: A relatively long, wide and thin piece of any material, usually wood or similar, often for use in construction or furniture-making.

boards.g: Examinations given for entry to college or to qualify for a profession.

boast.e: From Middle English bosten, from bost (“boast, glory, noise, arrogance, presumption, pride, vanity”), probably of North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“inflated, swollen, puffed up, proud, arrogant, bad”). Possible doublet of boost.
boast.g: A brag; ostentatious positive appraisal of oneself.

boastful.e: From Middle English bostful, equivalent to boast + -ful.

boat.e: From Middle English bot, boot, boet, boyt (“boat”), from Old English bāt (“boat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bait, from Proto-Germanic *baitaz, *baitą (“boat, small ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to break, split”) (whence also fissure via Latin).

bodily.e: From Middle English bodily; equivalent to body + -ly.
bodily.g: Of, relating to, or concerning the body.

body.e: From Middle English body, bodi, bodiȝ, from Old English bodiġ, bodeġ (“body, trunk, chest, torso, height, stature”), from Proto-West Germanic *bodag (“body, trunk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to be awake, observe”).

bodyguard.g: A person or group of persons, often armed, responsible for protecting someone.

boil.e: From Middle English bile, büle (“boil, tumor”), from Old English bȳl, bȳle (“boil, swelling”), from Proto-Germanic *būlijō, *būlō (“boil”). The expected form is bile; the rounding of the diphthong could be caused by the initial b- and/or by association with etymology 2.
boil.g: A localized accumulation of pus in the skin, resulting from infection.

boil.e: From Middle English boillen, from Old French boillir (see French bouillir) from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).
boil.g: The point at which fluid begins to change to a vapour; the boiling point.

boisterous.e: From Middle English boistres, an alteration of Middle English boistous (“crude, unrefined”), of uncertain origin. Likely from Anglo-Norman boystous, bustous (“rough, in a crude state, disabled, paralysed, unable to walk, lame”), Old French boitous (“limping; having a rough, uneven surface”).

bold.e: From Middle English bold, bolde, bald, beald, from Old English bald, beald (“bold, brave, confident, strong, of good courage, presumptuous, impudent”), from Proto-West Germanic *balþ, from Proto-Germanic *balþaz (“strong, bold”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-, *bʰlē- (“to bloat, swell, bubble”).
From Middle English bolden, balden, from Old English baldian, bealdian, from Proto-Germanic *balþōną, related to *balþaz (see above).
bold.g: To make (a font or some text) bold.

boldly.e: From Middle English boldely, boldeliche, baldeliche, from Old English bealdlīċe (“boldly, earnestly”), equivalent to bold + -ly.
boldly.g: In a bold manner; with confidence.

boldness.e: From Middle English boldnesse, equivalent to bold + -ness.
boldness.g: The state of being bold; courage.

boll.e: From Middle English bolle (“pod; shell”) and Middle Dutch bolle (“round object”), from Frankish *bollo, all ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bullô (“round object; bowl”).
boll.g: The rounded seed-bearing capsule of a cotton or flax plant.

bolster.e: From Middle English bolster, bolstre, from Old English bolster (“pillow”), from Proto-West Germanic *bolstr, from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz (“pillow, cushion”).
bolster.g: A large cushion or pillow, usually cylindrical in shape.

bolt.e: From Middle English bolt, from Old English bolt, from Proto-West Germanic *bolt, from Proto-Germanic *bultaz, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeld- (“to knock, strike”). The association of thunder and lightning with 'bolts' is found back into prehistory in many cultures, at least in Eurasia.
bolt.g: A (usually) metal fastener consisting of a cylindrical body that is threaded, with a larger head on one end. It can be inserted into an unth

bolt.e: From Middle English bulten, from Anglo-Norman buleter, Old French bulter (modern French bluter), from a Germanic source originally meaning "bag, pouch" cognate with Middle High German biuteln (“to sift”), from Proto-Germanic *buzdô (“beetle, grub, swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰūs- (“to move quickly”).
bolt.g: To sift, especially through a cloth.

bond.e: From Middle English bond, a variant of band, from Old English beand, bænd, bend (“bond, chain, fetter, band, ribbon, ornament, chaplet, crown”), from Proto-Germanic *bandaz, *bandiz (“band, fetter”)، from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie; bond, band”).
bond.g: A document constituting evidence of a long-term debt, by which the bond issuer (the borrower) is obliged to pay interest when due, and repay
To connect, secure or tie with a bond; to bind.

bondage.e: From Middle English bondage (“serfdom”), from British Medieval Latin bondagium (“an inferior tenure held by a bond or husbandman”), from Middle English bond (“tenant farmer, serf”), from Old English bonda (“householder, husband, head of a family”), of Old Norse origin. Sense development influenced by the unrelated terms bond and bind.
bondage.g: The state of being enslaved or the practice of slavery.

bondman.e: From Middle English bondman; equivalent to bond + -man.
bondman.g: A man who is bound in servitude.

bondwoman.e: From Middle English bondewomman; equivalent to bond + -woman.
bondwoman.g: A woman who is bound in servitude; a female slave.

bone.e: From Middle English bon, from Old English bān (“bone, tusk; the bone of a limb”), from Proto-Germanic *bainą (“bone”), from *bainaz (“straight”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to hit, strike, beat”).
bone.g: A composite material consisting largely of calcium phosphate and collagen and making up the skeleton of most vertebrates.

bone.e: Unknown; probably related in some way to Etymology 1, above.

bonnet.e: From Middle English bonet, from Middle French bonet (Modern French bonnet), from Old French bonet (“material from which hats are made”), from Frankish *bunni (“that which is bound”), from Proto-Germanic *bundiją (“bundle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”).
bonnet.g: A type of hat, once widely worn by women or children, held in place by ribbons tied under the chin; now uncommonly worn except in certain re

book.e: From Middle English book, bok, from Old English bōc, from Proto-Germanic *bōk, first and third person singular indicative past tense of Proto-Germanic *bakaną (“to bake”).

boot.e: From Middle English boote, bote (“shoe”), from Old French bote (“a high, thick shoe”). Of obscure origin, but probably related to Old French bot (“club-foot”), bot (“fat, short, blunt”), from Old Frankish *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz, *butaz (“cut off, short, numb, blunt”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewt-, *bʰewd- (“to strike, push, shock”).
boot.g: A heavy shoe that covers part of the leg.

boot.e: From Middle English boote, bote, bot, from Old English bōt (“help, relief, advantage”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōtu, from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“atonement, improvement”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰed- (“good”).

booth.e: From Middle English bothe, from Old East Norse *bóð, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō, *būþiz, *buþǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-.
booth.g: A small stall for the display and sale of goods.

booty.e: From Middle English buty, botye, bottyne, from Old French butin, botin, from Middle Low German bǖte (“distribution, exchange, loot”), of obscure origin, but related to Middle High German biute, German Beute (“booty”). Possibly ultimately from Proto-Celtic *boudi (“profit, gains; victory”). Sense perhaps influenced by boot (as in to boot).
booty.g: A form of prize which, when a ship was captured at sea, could be distributed at once.

booty.e: Probably an alteration of botty. Possibly influenced by booty (etymology 1).

border.e: From Middle English bordure, from Old French bordeure, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bord, equivalent to modern French bord (“a border”) + -er. Not cognate to beard, although inside Germanic there may have been influence between the senses of these two roots: see e.g. Old Norse barð (“edge”).
border.g: The line or frontier area separating political or geographical regions.

bore.e: From Middle English boren, from Old English borian (“to pierce”), from Proto-West Germanic *borōn, from Proto-Germanic *burōną. Sense of wearying may come from a figurative use such as "to bore the ears"; compare German drillen.
From Middle English *bore, bare, a borrowing from Old Norse bára (“billow, wave”), from Proto-Germanic *bērō (“that which bears or carries”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear”).
bore.g: A sudden and rapid flow of tide occurring in certain rivers and estuaries which rolls up as a wave.

born.e: From Middle English born, boren, borne, iborne, from Old English boren, ġeboren, from Proto-West Germanic *boran, *gaboran, from Proto-Germanic *buranaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *beraną (“to bear, carry”), equivalent to bear + -en.
born.g: Having from birth (or as if from birth) a certain quality or character; innate; inherited.

borne.e: From Middle English boren, iborne, from Old English boren, ġeboren, past participle of Old English beran (“to carry, bear”).

borrow.e: From Middle English borwen, from Old English borgian (“to borrow, lend, pledge surety for”), from Proto-West Germanic *borgōn, from Proto-Germanic *burgōną (“to pledge, take care of”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to take care”).
borrow.g: To receive (something) from somebody temporarily, expecting to return it.

borrow.e: From Middle English borwe, borgh, from Old English borh, borg, from Proto-West Germanic *borgōn, from Proto-Germanic *burgōną (“to borrow, lend”) (related to Etymology 1, above).
borrow.g: A ransom; a pledge or guarantee.

borrower.e: From Middle English borower, borewer, borwere, equivalent to borrow + -er (agent suffix).

bosom.e: From Middle English bosom, bosum, from Old English bōsm, from Proto-West Germanic *bōsm, from Proto-Germanic *bōsmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewH- (“to swell, bend, curve”). Related also to Albanian buzë (“lip”), Greek βυζί (vyzí, “breast”), Romanian buză (“lip”), Irish bus (“lip”), and Latin bucca (“cheek”).
bosom.g: The breast or chest of a human (or sometimes of another animal).

boss.e: Borrowed from Dutch baas, from Middle Dutch baes (“master of a household, friend”), from Old Dutch *baso (“uncle, kinsman”), from Proto-West Germanic *baswō, from Proto-Germanic *baswô (“uncle”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *ba-, *bō- (“father, older male relative”), source also of the English terms babe, boy, bub, bully.
boss.g: One who is in charge of something.
A hassock or small seat, especially made from a bundle of straw.

botch.e: From Middle English bocchen (“to mend”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old English bōtettan (“to improve; cure; remedy; repair”), related to boot, or from Middle Dutch botsen, butsen, boetsen (“to repair; patch”), related to beat.
botch.g: To perform (a task) in an incompetent or unacceptable manner; to make a mess of something.

botch.e: From Middle English botche, from Anglo-Norman boche, from Late Latin bocia (“boss”).
botch.g: A tumour or other malignant swelling.

both.e: From Middle English bothe, boþe, from Old English bā þā (“both the; both those”) and possibly reinforced by Old Norse báðir, from Proto-Germanic *bai. Replaced Middle English bō, from Old English bā, a form of Old English bēġen. A remnant of the Indo-European dual grammatical number.
both.g: Each of the two; one and the other; referring to two individuals or items.

bother.e: Borrowed from Scots bauther, bather (“to bother”). Origin unknown. Perhaps related to Scots pother (“to make a stir or commotion, bustle”), also of unknown origin. Perhaps related to Irish bodhaire (“noise”), Irish bodhraim (“to deafen, annoy”).
bother.g: To annoy, to disturb, to irritate; to be troublesome to, to make trouble for.

bottle.e: From Middle English botel (“bottle, flask, wineskin”), from Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula, diminutive of buttis (“cask”). Partially displaced Old English flasce.
bottle.g: A container, typically made of glass or plastic and having a tapered neck, used primarily for holding liquids.

bottle.e: From Middle English bottle, botel, buttle, from Old English botl (“building, house”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōþl, from Proto-Germanic *budlą, *buþlą, *bōþlą (“house, dwelling, farm”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (literally “to swell, grow, thrive, be, live, dwell”).

bottom.e: From Middle English botme, botom, from Old English botm, bodan (“bottom, foundation; ground, abyss”), from Proto-West Germanic *butm, from Proto-Germanic *butmaz, *budmaz (“bottom; ground”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”). The noun sense “posterior of a person” is first attested in 1794; the verb sense “to.

bottomless.e: From Middle English botemles, botmeles, equivalent to bottom + -less.

bough.e: From Middle English bough (“branch of a bush or tree, especially a main branch; limb of an animal or person; something resembling a branch (such as a plant root or branch of a nerve); (figuratively) Christian cross; descendant, offspring”), from Old English bōg, bōh (“tree bough or branch; arm; shoulder”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōgu.
bough.g: A tree-branch, usually a primary one directly attached to the trunk.

bought.e: From Middle English bought, bowght, bouȝt, *buȝt, probably an alteration of bight, biȝt, byȝt (“bend, bight”) after bowen, buwen, buȝen (“to bow, bend”).
bought.g: A bend; flexure; curve; a hollow angle.

bounce.e: From Middle English bounsen, bunsen (“to beat, thump”), cognate with Scots bunce, bonce (“to bounce”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps imitative, related to bump, or related to Middle English bonchen (“to pound, beat”) and Dutch bonken (“to bump”).
bounce.g: To change the direction of motion after hitting an obstacle.

bound.e: From Middle English bound, bund (preterite) and bounden, bunden, ibunden, ȝebunden (past participle), from Old English bund- and bunden, ġebunden respectively.

boundary.e: From bound + -ary. Semantically displaced native Old English mearc (“boundary, limit”) whence Modern English mark.
boundary.g: The dividing line or location between two areas.

bountiful.g: Having a quantity or amount that is generous or plentiful; ample.

bountifulness.e: From Middle English bountyffulnesse, equivalent to bountiful + -ness.

bounty.e: From Middle English bounte (“goodness, virtue; beauty; strength; chivalry, valour; excellence; kindness, mercy; good deed; generosity”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman bounté and Old French bonté, bontet, bunté (modern French bonté (“goodness, kindness”)), from Latin bonitās.
bounty.g: Generosity; also (countable) an act of generosity.

bow.e: From Middle English bowe, from Old English boga, Proto-West Germanic *bogō, from Proto-Germanic *bugô.
bow.g: A weapon made of a curved piece of wood or other flexible material whose ends are connected by a string, used for shooting arrows.

bow.e: From Middle English bowen, buwen, buȝen, from Old English būgan, from Proto-West Germanic *beugan, from Proto-Germanic *beuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewgʰ- (“to bend”).
bow.g: To bend oneself as a gesture of respect or deference.

bowel.e: Borrowed from Middle French bouel, from Old French boïel, from Latin botellus, diminutive of botulus (“sausage”).
bowel.g: A part or division of the intestines, usually the large intestine.

bowl.e: From Middle English bolle, from Old English bolla, bolle (“bowl, cup, pot, beaker, measure”), from Proto-West Germanic *bollā, from Proto-Germanic *bullǭ (“ball, round vessel, bowl”).
bowl.g: A roughly hemispherical container used to hold, mix, prepare or present food, such as salad, fruit or soup, or other items.

bowl.e: From Middle English bowle, boule, from Old French boule (“ball”), from Latin bulla (“bubble, stud, round object”).
bowl.g: The ball rolled by players in the game of lawn bowls.

bowlful.g: The amount that a bowl will hold.

bowshot.g: The act of firing an arrow from a bow.

bowstring.g: The string of an archer's bow.

box.e: From Middle English box (“container, box, cup”), from Old English box (“box, case”), from Proto-West Germanic *buhsā (“box”) from Late Latin buxis (“box”), Latin pyxis (“small box for medicines or toiletries”), of uncertain origin; compare Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís, “box or tablet made of boxwood; box; cylinder”) and πύξος (púxos, “box tree; boxwood”).
box.g: Senses relating to a three-dimensional object or space.

box.e: From Middle English box (“box tree; boxwood”), from Old English box (“box tree”), from Proto-West Germanic *buhs (“box tree; thing made from boxwood”), from Latin buxus (“box tree; thing made from boxwood”), buxum (“box tree; boxwood”), possibly from πύξος (púxos, “box tree; boxwood”).
box.g: Any of various evergreen shrubs or trees of genus Buxus, especially common box, European box, or boxwood (Buxus sempervirens) which is often

boxwood.e: From box + wood; box from Latin buxus (“box-tree, object made of boxwood”), of uncertain origin; compare Ancient Greek πύξος (púxos).

boy.e: From Middle English boy /boye (“servant, commoner, knave, boy”), from Old English *bōia (“boy”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōjō, from Proto-Germanic *bōjô (“younger brother, young male relation”), from Proto-Germanic *bō- (“brother, close male relation”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰā-, *bʰāt- (“father, elder brother, brother”).
